title: SIP routing table
description: Registrations, the lines they belong to, and the outbound routes that select one. These are the chart's values, so Helm checks them before templates/configmap.yaml renders routing.lua. Draft-07 with `definitions`, not 2020-12 with `$defs`: Helm's validator resolves no other dialect, and a 2020-12 schema is accepted and then enforces nothing.

sipfield.description: One field of a register line. No whitespace: the rendered table is TAB separated and read by `while read` in /bin/sh, so a tab or a newline here would split one entry into two.

linename.description: A line name. Lowercase, digits and hyphens, NO UNDERSCORE: it lands in a Matrix MXID localpart, where mautrix escapes a literal underscore to '=5f'. It must also differ from every SIP_TRUNKS host, or a '#<label>' destination would be ambiguous; tests/check-routing.py checks that against cheogram-sip.env.

address.description: A literal address. Never a pattern.

glob.description: An address pattern. '*' replaces the localpart only: xmpp:*@domain, matrix:@*:server. Bare 'xmpp:*' or 'matrix:*' is any user on that transport; '*' is anyone.

ring.description: Literal addresses rung simultaneously. A '*' here is rejected: you cannot ring a pattern.

record.description: Terminal stage: record a message instead of ringing.

transports.description: res_pjsip type=transport objects. Deployment facts, not per-trunk: nothing here varies with a registration, and an endpoint naming a transport this list does not define fails to load.

bind.description: <address>:<port>. The port is checked against what points at this Asterisk by tests/check-routing.py; a transport on another port is reachable from nothing.

trunk_transport.description: The transport every registration and endpoint generated from `registrations` rides. Must name one of `transports`.

external_address.description: The address the SDP must carry, on every transport: behind double NAT the pod address reaches nothing and audio goes nowhere. chan_sip's externip.

local_nets.description: The nets that are NOT behind external_address, so media to them keeps the pod address. chan_sip's localnet.

registrations.description: One outbound REGISTER per entry. The KEY IS THE WIRING: it is also the name of the Secret key holding that entry's password, mounted as a file under /sip-secrets. No password and no key name belongs in these values - they render into a plaintext ConfigMap, which scripts/check-substitution.py exists to keep credential-free. The pattern below is what makes the convention safe to state rather than transform: it is already a legal Kubernetes Secret key, so nothing is normalised at render time and a name that could not be one is rejected here at reconcile.

user.description: The carrier account, usually the DID in national form.

host.description: The registrar/proxy to REGISTER at. NOT the section an outbound call leaves by: the presented number is pinned per section, so every entry gets one of its own named after the ENTRY, and routing.lua carries that name as `peer`. Several entries may therefore share a host; what an inbound call is attributed to is the section, not this.

contact_user.description: PJSIP's registration/contact_user: what the carrier dials back, and therefore the extension an inbound call arrives on. It works only while the carrier echoes our registered Contact in the inbound Request-URI - observed behaviour, not a standard. Two entries sharing one on the same host make the dialled number invisible; tests/check-routing.py rejects that.

did.description: The dialled number: E.164 where it is globally routable, the provider's own form where it is not. Handed to the Matrix bridge as the recipient of an inbound SMS.

line.description: The line this registration belongs to. The ONLY statement of line membership - a line has no member list that could fall out of step with this.

entrypoint.description: This host's DEFAULT registration: the one an inbound call is attributed to when nothing identifies which DID was dialled, and so the only endpoint on that host that may carry a type=identify. At most one per host, or the fallback is undefined. Its user and host are also cheogram-sip.env's SIP_USER and SIP_HOST, which is what the component appends to a bare number.

peer_secret_file.description: Names the #include the initContainer writes this entry's password into, and pjsip.conf must #include it under exactly this name. Required: the object set is hand-written, so this is the only place a password can land.

lines.description: A line is an identity namespace: a caller reaching one is '<line>-<digits>' to Matrix and '+49...#<line>' to XMPP, and that XMPP form is also how a client dials back. A line name is therefore part of every portal key and every saved contact, and renaming one re-keys them. There is no default line - every line prefixes, so '#<host>' is not a line name and fails closed.

callers.description: WHO MAY PRESENT THIS IDENTITY: the outbound gate, and the only one. Checked on the line a destination resolved to, so it covers a labelled destination ('+49...#home') as well as one routed by the table. It REFUSES -- unlike from_glob it never falls through to another rule. An emergency route pins a registration rather than a line and so is not gated here, which is what keeps 110/112 reachable from an account that may dial nothing else.

primary.description: The registration this line speaks as outbound - Ofcom's Presentation Number, as against the Network Number the carrier transmits regardless. Must be a registration whose `line` is this one: a carrier may reject or silently rewrite a From the account does not own. Every other member rings in and is never presented. A line can only really present it once that registration has a peer of its own pinning fromuser to it, which is why tests/check-routing.py demands that of any line an outbound rule selects.

inbound_route.description: The line's call plan: ring stages tried in order until one answers. A 'record' stage must be last and, with no voicemail in the image, ends the call. Ring time is the SUM of the stages -- Asterisk times a whole Dial, never one target.

outbound.description: Ordered route table. FIRST MATCH WINS; the matched rule selects a line, whose primary registration yields both the peer the call leaves by and the number it presents.

to_pattern.description: A LUA PATTERN matched against the destination, auto-anchored by the renderer as ^(...)$ so '11[02]' cannot also match '0112345'. Asterisk's Lua 5.1 has no regex engine, so the regex-only characters { } | and backslash are rejected here: a regex written by mistake would not error, it would match nothing and the call would silently fall through to the next rule. Repetition counts are spelled out, '%d%d?%d?' for one to three digits. It matches only and cannot rewrite the dialled string; a carrier that ever needs a dial-out prefix gets a field on the registration rather than a pattern that edits.

from_glob.description: Optional. NARROWS a rule to certain callers, which is how a per-person default line is expressed: put their rule above the general one. Any entry matching is a match. It FALLS THROUGH -- a caller it excludes is not refused, the next rule decides. Permission is `lines.<name>.callers`, never this.

registration.description: Pins one registration, bypassing the line's presented number. Only an emergency rule may do this, and the two are required together.

emergency.description: Emergency route. Skips the outbound permission check, and pins the registration whose registered address the dispatcher is handed - the presented number is what fixes that address, and Sec. 120(2) TKG permits presenting only a number a Nutzungsrecht exists for.
